notes.meaning: Jesus traveled up to Jerusalem to attend a Jewish religious feast. Going to the festival showed His respect for God's law and gave Him an opportunity to teach the large crowds of worshippers gathered there.

Near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem stood a pool named Bethesda, surrounded by five covered porches. Its name means 'house of mercy,' and its shelters gave shade and resting space to crowds of sick and weak people.
A large number of sick people lay under these covered walkways, including those who were blind, lame, and paralyzed. They stayed near the pool hoping to receive healing when the water was stirred.

In the traditional reading, an angel of the Lord came down at certain times to stir the water, and the first person to step in was healed of any illness. This showed God's supernatural power and mercy toward suffering people, preparing their hearts for the coming Messiah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that this verse is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts, suggesting it was originally an explanatory note written in the margin by a scribe.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers treat the stirred water as a pattern for physical points of contact in prayer, while others claim God is releasing similar healing pools around the world today.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers saw the stirred water as a symbol pointing forward to Christian baptism, where the Holy Spirit works with water to heal the soul.

notes.meaning: One man lying there had suffered from his disabling condition for thirty-eight years. His illness was of very long standing, leaving him weak and without any human hope of recovery.
Jesus saw the man lying on his mat and knew he had been sick for a very long time. He asked him if he wanted to get well, awakening the man's attention, hope, and desire for healing.

The man explained that he had no friend to carry him into the pool when the water moved, and someone else always stepped in ahead of him. His answer showed his helplessness and how he limited God's help only to what he could imagine.

Jesus commanded the man to stand up, pick up his sleeping mat, and walk. Christ gave the order and supplied the power to obey it, showing that His spoken word can heal directly without any pool of water.
The man was cured immediately, rolled up his mat, and began to walk. This complete miracle took place on the Sabbath, the Jewish weekly day of rest, setting off a conflict with the religious rulers.

The Jewish religious leaders confronted the healed man and told him that carrying his mat broke the Sabbath law. They focused strictly on external regulations about carrying burdens rather than rejoicing over his amazing recovery.

The man answered that the very person who made him completely well had ordered him to pick up his mat and walk. He rightly reasoned that someone with the divine authority to heal him had full right to tell him what to do.

The leaders demanded to know who told him to pick up his mat and walk. They deliberately skipped over the miracle of his healing and searched only for a person to punish for breaking their Sabbath traditions.

The healed man did not know who Jesus was, because Jesus had quietly slipped away into the crowd. Jesus stepped away to avoid public praise and to let the miracle stand on its own before facing His opponents.

Jesus later found the man at the temple and told him to stop sinning so that nothing worse would happen to him. Jesus showed that He cared for the man's soul, warning him that returning to sin could bring greater misery or eternal judgment.
The man went and reported to the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who had restored his health. He told them about his healer, likely intending to give credit to Jesus rather than cause Him harm.

The religious authorities began persecuting Jesus and sought to kill Him because He healed people on the Sabbath day. Their strict legal rules blinded them to God's love, leading them to hate the One doing good in their midst.

Jesus answered their charges by declaring that His Father never stops working to sustain life and do good, and He works alongside Him. Because God continually upholds creation on the Sabbath, Jesus has the divine right to heal on that day as well.

This reply made the leaders try even harder to kill Him, because He not only broke their Sabbath rules but called God His own Father. By calling God His Father in this unique way, Jesus claimed to be equal with God in nature and power.

Jesus explained that the Son does not act independently or apart from the Father, but only does what He sees the Father doing. Because Father and Son share the same divine nature and purpose, the Son carries out the Father's works in the exact same way.

The Father loves the Son and hides nothing from Him, showing Him everything He is doing. Jesus told them that the Father would show Him even greater works than this healing, which would leave His listeners amazed.

Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever He wishes. Jesus claimed the sovereign power that belongs only to God, having full authority to give both physical and spiritual life.

The Father does not directly judge people, but has given all authority to judge into the hands of the Son. Entrusting all judgment to Jesus demonstrates His divine wisdom and right to decide the eternal outcome of every person.

God gave this authority to the Son so that everyone would honor the Son with the same worship and reverence due to the Father. Anyone who refuses to honor the Son dishonors the Father who sent Him into the world.

Jesus promised that whoever hears His word and trusts the Father who sent Him has eternal life right now. Believers will not face final condemnation, because they have already moved out of spiritual death into everlasting life.

differ.view: True believers are permanently secure in Christ, and once they cross from death to life they will persevere to the end.
A believer is given eternal life when they trust Christ, but that gift can be lost if a person later makes shipwreck of their faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Eternal life is a real present gift through faith, but salvation is not guaranteed unconditionally and can be forfeited if a person falls into grave sin.
